title: Solar Closing Desk for Listing Agents
one_liner: A per-listing service that clears solar leases, PPAs, loans and UCC-1 fixture filings before the house hits the MLS, so escrow does not blow up in week three.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and title/escrow firms in solar-dense counties (CA, AZ, FL, TX, NJ, MA, CO, NV, HI). The seller pays $395-795 per listing at closing from proceeds, or a brokerage pays a flat subscription.
problem: Solar lease and PPA transfers need provider consent, which can add 2-6 weeks to escrow and sometimes fails. Solar UCC-1 fixture filings show up on the title prelim and block closings, refinances and HELOCs. Agents usually discover this on day 20 of escrow, when the buyer's credit check fails or the provider's transfer queue stalls. One industry cite claims about half of agents have had solar complicate a deal. The 2015-2020 lease vintages are now entering resale years, and TPO is the only route to a federal credit since 2026, so volume rises for a decade.
solution: Start the clock at listing, not at contract. Within 48 hours, identify who owns the system using permit data, UCC search, the title prelim and a monitoring-account check. Order the provider's payoff and transfer packet. Soft-pre-qualify likely buyers in the provider's portal. Produce a one-page Solar Fact Sheet for the MLS with verified production history, remaining term, escalator and buyout cost. Then run the chosen path: payoff and UCC-3 termination, transfer with consent, or subordination to the new mortgage. Provide escrow instructions and agent scripts, and offer buyout financing through a partner.
why_now: TPO has become the dominant way to buy solar after 25D ended. First-wave lease systems are hitting the resale market, provider servicing is in flux after the Sunnova and SunPower failures (successor servicer SunStrong), and title companies are seeing more fixture-filing holds. Home sales are slow, so agents cannot afford failed escrows.
revenue_model: Flat per-listing fee paid at closing. Referral fee from lease-buyout lenders (about 1% of buyout). White-label subscription for title and escrow companies. Later, sell aggregated solar-adjustment data to appraisers and mortgage investors.
non_obvious_insight: Every provider's transfer team is a queue with known choke points: the buyer's credit pull, the time-limited buyer acceptance window, and UCC-3 termination filing lag. An installer sees this because neighbors' failed sales kill sales for the next solar rep. The fix is operational, not legal. Agents cannot price a lease because they cannot read production guarantees or escalators, so a plain fact sheet makes the solar a selling point instead of a discount.
first_30_days: Interview 15 listing agents in one solar-heavy county. Offer 5 active solar listings handled free in exchange for testimonials. Hire a part-time escrow officer or paralegal. Publish a Solar Home Sale Checklist for agents to get inbound leads. Sign a pilot with two local title companies. Use manual processes and one shared spreadsheet, with no software build until 50 listings.

title: Condition-Based Kitchen Exhaust Cleaning Sensors
one_liner: Duct-mounted grease-film sensor pods, sold through hood-cleaning contractors, that predict when a restaurant's exhaust system actually needs cleaning and prove the cleaning was done.
customer: Independent commercial kitchen exhaust cleaning contractors (5-50 technicians) as the channel and first payer. End users are restaurants, hotels, hospital and campus kitchens, and ghost-kitchen operators, with commercial property insurers as a downstream discount payer.
problem: NFPA 96 sets calendar cleaning intervals from monthly to annual by cooking type, but real grease buildup varies enormously by menu (wok, charbroil and fryer kitchens versus sandwich shops). The result is over-cleaning in some places and dangerous under-cleaning in others. Restaurants can't see inside their ducts, so they can't verify that hard-to-reach plenum and duct runs were really cleaned. Grease is a leading cause of restaurant fires and property insurers increasingly want documentation.
solution: A retrofit pod at the hood plenum and an access panel, with temperature, airflow or differential-pressure, fan-current and a capacitive grease-film sensor. It uses BLE or LoRa to a small gateway. An edge model outputs 'days to cleaning threshold' and schedules the contractor. After each cleaning the pod records a post-clean baseline, which becomes tamper-evident proof for the restaurant, the fire inspector and the insurer. Start with sensors outside the duct interior (plenum, access panel) to avoid grease and heat survivability problems.
why_now: Cheap MEMS and capacitive sensing plus LoRa/BLE make a sub-USD-100 pod feasible. Documentation expectations in recent NFPA 96 editions and commercial property insurance hardening push restaurants toward provable maintenance. Contractors face thin margins and want stickier recurring contracts.
revenue_model: Hardware at USD 180-350 per hood, or leased. Subscription of USD 25-45 per month per hood, with a 30% revenue share to the contractor who resells and installs. Pilot insurer premium-credit program. Contractor-side scheduling and route-optimization software as an upsell.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the cleaner, not the restaurant. Monitoring turns a commodity route-calendar service into a data-backed recurring contract and cuts wasted truck rolls. The most valuable reading is not the continuous alert but the after-clean baseline, because the actual pain is 'did they really clean the duct?' That is a trust problem no one solves today.
first_30_days: Prototype a pod from off-the-shelf sensors. Recruit three cleaning contractors through the International Kitchen Exhaust Cleaning Association network and offer free pods on 10 hoods each. Log grease-accumulation curves by cuisine type for 60-90 days. Show the contractors their own before/after evidence, then sell the first paid subscriptions with revenue share.

title: Bonded Escorts for Sedated Outpatient Patients
one_liner: A background-checked adult who legally receives your discharge instructions and takes you home after a colonoscopy or other sedated procedure, sold to the clinics that lose the slot when you have no ride.
customer: Independent GI groups and ambulatory surgery centers pay $65-95 per escorted visit. Solo agers and estranged or far-from-family adults pay $99-149 directly as a fallback.
problem: Most sedation centers will not proceed unless a responsible adult picks the patient up and hears the discharge instructions, and many refuse to release a sedated patient to a rideshare driver. Patients with no spouse, no nearby family, or no friend willing to sit through the aftermath of a bowel prep cancel, delay screening, or no-show. The clinic eats an empty high-margin slot. The patient feels embarrassed to ask and avoids the procedure.
solution: A regional network of vetted, insured escorts drawn from CNAs, retired nurses, EMTs and nursing students. The clinic scheduler adds one line to the booking call: 'No escort? Tap here and we will send one.' The escort meets the patient at the door, is named on the chart as the responsible adult, receives instructions, rides home with the patient, stays 20-30 minutes until the patient is settled, and texts a family contact. A clinic dashboard shows escort confirmed, so day-of cancellations for this reason disappear. Later add the required 24-hour post-anesthesia overnight companion, then cataract, oral surgery, and cosmetic and orthopedic day surgery.
why_now: The USPSTF lowered the colorectal screening start age to 45, which added millions of eligible patients. Procedures keep migrating to ambulatory surgery centers, which run on tight slot economics. The share of older adults living alone (solo agers) is at a record high. Checkr-style vetting and Stripe Connect-style payouts let a tiny team stand up a bonded, insured gig network in weeks. No incumbent sells 'the adult on the chart' to schedulers.
revenue_model: Per-visit fee paid by the clinic ($65-95, escort keeps about 60%) or patient-pay ($99-149). Add-ons include overnight post-anesthesia sitters billed hourly. Later, Medicare Advantage plans buy escort-with-transport as a supplemental benefit.
non_obvious_insight: The escort rule is a liability policy, not a medical one, so what the clinic needs is a credentialed name on the chart that satisfies the discharge nurse, not a ride. Nobody sells to the scheduling desk, where the cancellation leak is measured in dollars per slot. The patient's real barrier is shame at asking a friend to witness a colonoscopy, which a professional stranger removes.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Recruit 15 escorts from nursing-school boards and retired-nurse groups. Get a general and professional liability quote and run Checkr checks. Visit 10 GI practices and offer a free 30-day pilot where they pay only when an escort saves a slot that would have cancelled. Launch a landing page and a Twilio text line, and buy Google Ads on searches like 'colonoscopy no one to drive me home'. Run dispatch from a spreadsheet. Goal: 40 escorted procedures and 3 signed clinics.

title: Fry-Oil Co-op Escaping Evergreen Renderer Contracts
one_liner: Aggregate independent restaurants' used cooking oil, sell it to biofuel buyers at market with sensor-verified traceability, and hand the owner the check the big renderer keeps.
customer: Independent restaurants and small chains with 2-20 fryer-heavy units are the supply side and pay no fee. Local independent oil collectors, biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF feedstock processors and brokers are the demand side and pay the co-op. Revenue is the spread plus a small sensor rental fee.
problem: Used fry oil is a commodity that biofuel makers have been bidding up, yet independents are locked into 3-year auto-renewing pickup contracts with a large renderer or bin company. The restaurant is paid a pittance or nothing, or is even charged fees. Bins overflow, which brings health-code and odor problems. Thieves steal oil at night, and nobody reconciles what the oil is actually worth. Owners don't switch because the termination window is a 60-90 day certified-letter deadline buried in the contract, and nobody has time to run a bid.
solution: A co-op platform that: (1) tracks each member's contract renewal date and files the non-renewal notice on time; (2) runs a monthly reverse auction among local collectors so that volume, not the restaurant, gets the price; (3) installs a roughly $40 ultrasonic fill sensor and a lockable tank cap, so pickups trigger at 80% full and every pickup is photo- or QR-verified; (4) issues a statement per pickup indexed to a published used-cooking-oil price series; and (5) produces per-restaurant chain-of-custody records that renewable-fuel producers need to prove domestic, traceable feedstock.
why_now: As I understand it, federal clean-fuel incentives (45Z) now favor North American feedstock, and concern about mislabeled imported used oil has raised the value of traceable domestic oil. Renewable diesel and SAF capacity keeps growing. Cheap cellular fill sensors are widely available. Restaurants' margins are so thin that any found cash gets attention. Verify the current feedstock price index and the 45Z sourcing rules before you pitch.
revenue_model: 20-30% spread on oil sold, indexed and transparent, plus $10-30 per month for the sensor and tank lock. Later add a premium for verified-traceable oil sold to fuel producers, and carbon-intensity documentation fees.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbent's real product is the locked contract and route density, not the oil service, so the way in is the calendar rather than a better price. The contract renewal date is the CRM key: a 90-day-out certified non-renewal letter, filed for the owner, is the growth engine. Owners think they are getting 'free removal', so nobody shops it. Also, per-restaurant traceability is worth more to fuel buyers than the oil's volume alone.
first_30_days: Walk one restaurant row and photograph each bin's contract label, and note the pickup company and renewal date for 40 restaurants in one metro. Sign one local collector or small biodiesel maker as a buyer with a written price index. Enroll 8-10 off-contract or month-to-month members, including my own two locations. Install sensors and lock caps, run the first monthly auction, and show each owner a side-by-side statement of what their old vendor paid versus what the co-op did.

title: Arc-Flash and Protection Studies Factory
one_liner: Deliver PE-stamped short-circuit, coordination and arc-flash studies in days rather than months, using AI to turn photos and one-lines into models.
customer: Electrical contractors and EPCs building C&I storage, EV depots and data center electrical rooms, plus facility managers facing five-year label refreshes.
problem: Power-systems engineers are scarce and studies gate energization and permits, with 8-12 week backlogs. A delayed 60 MW site costs about $3M a week. NFPA 70E requires reassessment every five years, and small C&I storage projects cannot afford $30k custom studies.
solution: Studies as a productized service. The contractor uploads single-line diagrams, nameplate photos and the utility fault-current letter. AI extracts the equipment and builds the ETAP or SKM model, a licensed PE reviews and stamps it, and the customer gets labels and coordination settings on a five-business-day SLA at a flat price per switchboard.
why_now: Vision and language models now parse one-lines and nameplates well enough to draft models. The data center and storage boom, and the engineer shortage, make throughput the scarce resource.
revenue_model: $3-15k per small C&I study, $30-100k per data center study, and recurring five-year renewals plus label printing.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody lacks software. They lack stamps and turnaround time. PE-supervised throughput with AI drafts is a labor arbitrage that stays unglamorous enough to avoid heavy competition.
first_30_days: Recruit two retired power-systems PEs. Build the extraction pipeline on 20 anonymized one-lines. Sell five C&I storage installers a $4k fixed-price study with a five-day SLA. Measure margins.

title: Supplier-Owned Origin Passport for Tier-2 Shops
one_liner: A portable, supplier-owned origin and metal-content passport that answers every customer's questionnaire once.
customer: Tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers with 10-200 employees in the US, Mexico and Canada. Buyers pay for portfolio dashboards.
problem: USMCA was not renewed on 2026-07-01 and now faces annual reviews through 2036. USTR flagged simplified compliance for smaller suppliers. CBP is prioritizing origin verification. Full-value duties depend on HTS class, metal weight and melt origin per SKU. Every buyer sends a different spreadsheet, and small suppliers re-answer them all with errors that expose buyers to penalties.
solution: Guided intake for BOM, mill certs (melt and pour country extracted from MTR PDFs), HTS and USMCA tariff-shift or regional-content calculation, kept as a versioned, signed record. The supplier shares subsets with each buyer by link. Buyers get standardized machine-readable packets and alerts when rules change. The first buyer is free, and suppliers pay to share with more.
why_now: Annual USMCA reviews create a permanent audit cycle, CBP is focused on origin verification, and Section 232 tiers now depend on melt origin. Regulators are asking for less burdensome small-supplier compliance.
revenue_model: $99-299 a month per supplier. $5-25k a year per buyer for dashboards and change alerts. Enterprise connectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Existing tools are sold to buyers and force suppliers into each buyer's portal. A supplier-owned credential flips the network effect, like a Plaid for origin. The USTR note on smaller suppliers signals regulators want a reusable format.
first_30_days: Target one cluster, such as 40 suppliers of one mid-size OEM in Monterrey/Laredo or Ohio. Get that OEM's buyer to say it will accept the passport. Build LLM extraction for mill certs. Onboard manually and aim for 10 paying suppliers.

title: Servicer-Funded Nonrenewal Rescue Agent for Homeowners
one_liner: When a homeowner's policy is nonrenewed, an agent contests the machine-made underwriting flag, documents mitigation and reshops 30 carriers plus the FAIR plan, paid by the mortgage servicer that would otherwise face a coverage lapse.
customer: Mortgage servicers and credit-union lenders pay per rescued loan; homeowners get the service free; a licensed partner agency earns placement commission.
problem: Homeowner nonrenewals are at records (a record 6,200 in New Mexico, Utah highest in 2025), premiums now rival mortgage payments, and California just passed three nonrenewal and claims bills (2026-09-03). Reinsurance is softening and cat bonds are at record issuance, yet primary policyholders see none of it. Carriers increasingly rely on aerial-imagery and AI scores (roof condition, overhanging trees, tarps) that are often wrong or fixable for a few hundred dollars, and homeowners have no one to contest a machine or work 30 quote portals.
solution: On a nonrenewal or a 25%+ renewal spike (detected from escrow data), a consumer-side agent gathers the stated reason, pulls imagery evidence where the state requires disclosure, and assembles a rebuttal or cure package (photos, contractor invoices, mitigation credits). In parallel it runs quotes across carrier and FAIR-plan portals acting as the user, and a licensed partner agency binds coverage. The servicer sees coverage status in a dashboard.
why_now: Nonrenewals are at records and states are adding rules. Softening reinsurance leaves carriers room to take documented risk back. Agentic browsers acting as the user now have appellate support (Ninth Circuit, 2026-08-04). Servicers face lapse, force-placed coverage and delinquency risk as insurance stress rises.
revenue_model: $100-250 per rescued loan from the servicer, 8-15% placement commission through the licensed agency, and contractor referral fees for cure work.
non_obvious_insight: The person in pain cannot pay, but the party whose collateral and cash flow depend on continuous coverage can. The counterparty is now a machine, so the rescue has to run at machine speed and machine cost: dollars per case for an agent versus hours for a human broker is what makes a $150 servicer fee profitable.
first_30_days: Pick one state (Colorado, Utah or Oklahoma). Partner with one credit union or regional servicer and run a free pilot on about 200 borrowers with nonrenewal notices, which they see in escrow analysis. Work the first 20 cases semi-manually with a licensed agency partner, track reinstatement and placement rates and cost per case, then quote the servicer a per-rescue fee.

title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.
revenue_model: A fee of about 1-1.75% per advance cycle, which works out to roughly 15-25% annualized, plus a $99 a month reconciliation subscription. Contingency of about 10% on missing refunds recovered. Later, sell or syndicate the receivables to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: To a bank this looks like distress lending to a struggling small business. In reality it is close to prime paper: the obligor is a drug manufacturer with a statutory duty to pay, routed through a federal facilitator, backed by claim-level data. Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'find my missing refunds' report to 25 pharmacies through state association newsletters and pharmacy owner Facebook groups. Line up a $500k credit line from a regional bank or family office and keep the first ten advances small. Talk to a fintech attorney about commercial-financing disclosure laws by state. Approach one PSAO about distribution.

title: Half-Pro Remodeling: Homeowner Does the Easy 60%
one_liner: Fixed-price booking of only the licensed, permit-required slice of a project while homeowners or handymen do demo, prep and finish, with photo-verified handoffs.
customer: Budget-constrained homeowners with $3-15K bath, kitchen, water-heater, mini-split and electrical projects. Supply side: solo licensed plumbers and electricians who want prequalified, ready-to-work half-day jobs.
problem: Angi data shows 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects and 72% of postponers cite budget. The average project is $5,368. DIY-only fell from 50% to 39% while homeowner-plus-pro rose from 27% to 46%. Pros say they are too busy and skip small, messy, scope-uncertain jobs. Platforms sell whole jobs, so homeowners get no quotes.
solution: A catalog of standardized pro steps: rough-in for a vanity swap, shutoff valve and supply lines, gas line, water heater swap, ceiling-fan or lighting circuit, mini-split hookup, permit pull and inspection sign-off. Each comes with a homeowner checklist (nine prep steps, three photos) checked by a vision model, and a pro shows up for a fixed price to a job that is actually ready. Start only where owner-builder and licensing rules are clear.
why_now: Angi's 2026 backlog data. Credit cards rose to 30% of project payments. 62% now choose repair over replace. Contractors are capacity-constrained. Multimodal models can verify prep photos cheaply.
revenue_model: 15-20% take on the pro-step price ($300-1,500), plus materials affiliate margin from a local supply house. Pros pay nothing upfront.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of demand is not the project, it is the licensed hour. The blended-work data says homeowners do not want turnkey, they want to transfer risk only on the parts they legally or practically cannot do. Nobody sells the licensed two hours with a photo-checked handoff, and small pros love the productivity of arriving at a ready job.
first_30_days: One metro, four job types. Recruit 10 solo plumbers and electricians from local trade Facebook groups. Launch a landing page with local ads. Run 30 bookings by hand with a spreadsheet and Stripe.

title: Employer-Backed Workforce Pell Program Packager
one_liner: Package 8-15 week, employer-guaranteed training programs that clear state approval and the 70% completion and 70% placement tests, paid per verified hire by the employers who need workers, with Pell covering tuition.
customer: Employers with chronic shortages (HVAC contractors, utilities and lineworker programs, hospitals for phlebotomy, CNA and sterile processing, machine shops, CDL trucking) paying per hire. Community and technical colleges are the Title IV-eligible partners.
problem: Workforce Pell (from 1 July 2026) opens Pell Grants to 150-599 clock-hour programs. A governor and state workforce board must approve each program as aligned to high-skill, high-wage, in-demand jobs, and programs must show at least 70% completion and 70% job placement plus a tuition-versus-earnings test. Colleges' continuing-ed divisions lack employer partnerships, placement tracking and approval paperwork skills. ED approved its first programs in mid-Sept 2026 (Nebraska, Texas, North Carolina) and 36 jurisdictions have an operating process.
solution: Act as a program packager and placement-assurance layer, not a tuition-share OPM, given the Title IV incentive-compensation rules. Steps: co-design the syllabus from employer job tasks; assemble the state approval dossier with employer letters and labor-market data; give the college cohort software covering employer offer commitments contingent on completion, completion nudges, and 180-day placement tracking via payroll and wage-record attestations; and bill employers per successful hire rather than per enrollment.
why_now: The program is only weeks old, states are just standing up approval processes, and the outcome thresholds will remove weak programs. Colleges need employer-tethered programs that can actually hit the 70/70 tests.
revenue_model: $2,000-$6,000 per hire from employers (well below typical 15-25% agency fees), $1-3k/month per college for cohort and placement software, and fixed fees for approval dossiers.
non_obvious_insight: The outcome test flips the customer. The college's real risk is the 70% placement rate, and only an employer that pre-commits to hire can guarantee it, so the payer is the employer rather than the student or school. Pell effectively becomes a federal training subsidy for whichever employers organize demand first.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a live approval process and shortages (Texas, North Carolina or Nebraska) and one sector such as HVAC, lineworker or sterile processing. Collect 5 employer hiring commitments and co-apply with 1-2 community colleges for a 10-week program. Run a non-Pell pilot cohort while approval is pending to test placement, and have counsel review the incentive-compensation boundary.

title: Flat-Fee Authenticity Reports for Family-Law Attorneys
one_liner: 48-hour, court-ready analyses of disputed audio, video and screenshots at $400-900, instead of $10K expert engagements.
customer: Solo and small-firm family-law, employment and landlord-tenant attorneys, HR investigators, school districts, and small police departments.
problem: Fake voicemails, cloned-voice threats and doctored screenshots now appear as evidence in custody and workplace disputes, and real evidence gets dismissed as fake. Forensic experts cost $5-15K and take weeks, which prices out most cases. Evidence-rule committees are debating standards for machine-generated evidence.
solution: Upload a file for automated provenance checks (metadata, re-encoding traces, C2PA), multi-detector analysis, voice consistency against known samples, and platform-screenshot forensics. A human examiner reviews and signs, and the output is a plain-language report, declaration template, methodology and error-rate disclosure.
why_now: Voice cloning takes 3 seconds of audio, which floods lower-stakes disputes with synthetic-evidence claims. Courts are asking who verified the evidence, and no one serves the long tail of small cases.
revenue_model: $400-900 per report, $299 per month for firms including 3 reports, and expert-testimony upsells at about $3K.
non_obvious_insight: The market is not detection accuracy but the cost of access to a credentialed examiner. Demand is two-sided: people accused of faking real evidence also need authenticity certificates. The human sign-off is the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 contract forensic examiners. Build the intake page and report template. Run bar-association webinars and get 10 family-law firms to buy 3 pilot reports each.

title: The Neutral Verdict on Dad's Driving
one_liner: An independent on-road evaluation of an aging parent's driving that gives adult children a credentialed Green, Yellow or Red verdict, plus a graduated plan so nobody has to be the villain about the keys.
customer: Adult children aged 45-65 of drivers 75+ pay $349-449 per evaluation and $12 a month for monitoring. Later buyers are auto insurers, Medicare Advantage plans and long-term-care insurers.
problem: Taking away the keys is one of the most dreaded family confrontations. The parent hears loss of independence and the child becomes the villain. Doctors rarely intervene, DMV medical review is slow, and driver-rehab specialists have months-long waitlists. Families wait for a crash. AAA and AARP offer generic tips, not an individual, defensible verdict.
solution: Frame it as a safety tune-up and send a certified evaluator, an OT with driver-rehab credentials or trained retired instructors under OT supervision. They ride in the parent's own car on a standardized 45-minute route with scoring for gap judgment, lane keeping, hesitation and scanning, plus a brief cognitive screen. The report gives a Green, Yellow or Red verdict. Yellow means no night, highway or rush hour with a recheck in six months, optionally verified by connected-car data or a cheap OBD dongle with the parent's consent. Red comes with a transition kit of robotaxi and rideshare credits, grocery and pharmacy delivery, and a senior-center pass, so retirement feels like an upgrade. The evaluator is advisory only and DMV referral is optional.
why_now: The oldest baby boomers turn 80 in 2026. Robotaxis now operate commercially in a growing list of US metros, so a real off-ramp finally exists. Connected-car APIs make objective driving data possible with consent. Scarce driver-rehab specialists can be leveraged with standardized scoring and remote review.
revenue_model: $349-449 per evaluation, a $12 monthly monitoring subscription for Yellow-zone drivers, and referral or ride-credit margin on the transition kit. B2B per-evaluation contracts with insurers and Medicare Advantage plans that want fewer elder-driver claims.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a third party who absorbs the blame. Families are buying relational insurance, not a road test. The recurring money is in the Yellow zone, where a graduated restriction plan needs ongoing verification, which turns a one-off confrontation into a subscription.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 driver-rehab OTs in one metro, plus elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers for referrals. Build the scoring sheet from published road-test protocols. Get liability coverage and a consent script. Run 10 evaluations at a $249 intro price. Recruit through caregiver-support groups and Facebook groups for adult children of aging parents. Publish anonymized case studies.

title: Transition Sponsor Radar for Strategic Breakthrough Awards
one_liner: A subscription and dossier service that maps each SBIR Phase II technology to the specific budget line, program office and person who could commit to a Program Objective Memorandum (POM), which the new $30M Strategic Breakthrough awards require.
customer: Phase II awardees in DoD-funded SBIR (thousands per year) that want Phase III or Strategic Breakthrough money, plus SBIR-focused VCs and advisors who decide which portfolio companies to back.
problem: Strategic Breakthrough awards run up to $30M over 48 months, but a company needs at least one prior Phase II, at least 100% matching funds from new private capital or non-SBIR government money, and, for DoD, a 'commitment for inclusion in a program objective memorandum' from the acquisition executive or higher. Agencies must contract within 90 days of a proposal. The technology is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is finding the one person with authority over a budget line, and knowing the POM calendar, since the POM is written 18 to 24 months ahead of the fiscal year. The public data (R-1/R-2 RDT&E exhibits, P-1 procurement lines, FPDS contracts, SBIR.gov awards) exists but is not indexed by technology.
solution: Build a searchable graph linking SBIR.gov Phase II abstracts to R-2 program elements, project numbers and named PEOs/PMs, and to FPDS Phase III contracts (where SBIR data-rights clauses appear). For each customer, produce a 'sponsor dossier': the top 5 program elements that could absorb the tech, the POM cycle dates, who to call, precedent Phase III transitions, and candidate match-fund sources. Add a monthly alert when a relevant program element grows or a new Phase III model contract appears.
why_now: The Strategic Breakthrough allocation (up to 0.50% of an agency's R&D budget where R&D exceeds $100M) takes effect in FY2026 and runs to September 30, 2031. Agencies must also create standardized Phase I/II/III model contracts and track direct-to-Phase-II, strategic breakthrough and Phase III awards in the database. Data on where transitions happen will become far richer as this reporting starts.
revenue_model: $12k to $20k per tech-specific sponsor dossier, paid partly from the $50k Phase II T&BA allowance. $1,500 per month subscription for alerts and updates. $5k per month for SBIR-focused VC funds screening deals. Success fee on Phase III wins (1% to 3%) as an optional add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not funding, it is a named budget-holder who will put a line in a POM, and that map is buildable from public documents no one has joined to SBIR data. S. 3971 Section 3 (new Section 9(ff)(3)) sets the $30M cap, 48-month term, one prior Phase II, 100% match, DoD POM-commitment requirement and 90-day contracting deadline. Section 6 requires 'simplified and standardized procedures and model contracts' for Phase III. Section 8 requires the database to track Phase III prime and subcontract awards. All at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm. The award-size thresholds the SBA gave for April 2026 ($323,090 Phase I, $2,153,927 Phase II without SBA approval, https://www.sbir.gov/about) show how small the normal awards are next to a $30M award, so the sponsor commitment becomes the step everyone is scrambling for.
first_30_days: Download the SBIR.gov awards dataset and the latest DoD RDT&E R-2 exhibits (comptroller.defense.gov). Use an LLM to embed and match 200 recent Phase II abstracts to program elements, then have a former acquisition officer sanity-check the top matches. Give 10 Phase II founders a free one-page 'sponsor map' for their own tech. Convert 3 of them to a $12k dossier. Pitch 2 SBIR-focused VC funds a paid pilot on their portfolio.

title: Walkable Childhood Homes for Memory Care
one_liner: Generate explorable 3D versions of a person's childhood street, lost home or homeland from a few photos and stories, delivered on a TV or tablet for memory care, hospice and diaspora families.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living communities (activity budgets), hospices and adult children, paying $250-600 per scene or $300-600 a month per community.
problem: Reminiscence is among the best-supported non-drug interventions for dementia and late-life low mood, but the props are still photos and music. Existing VR programs offer generic 'visit Paris' content, not personal places. Immigrants, refugees and the bereaved have no visual way back to a home that no longer exists.
solution: A studio workflow: family interview intake, photo and archival-map collection, a world-model pipeline that builds an era-appropriate walkable scene, and a docent mode where staff or grandchildren ask 'what was on this corner?'. Human artists finalize each scene to remove uncanny or distressing artifacts, and a gentle mode limits sensory intensity.
why_now: Generative world models released in 2025 (Google's Genie 3, World Labs' Marble and similar) can create persistent, explorable scenes from a handful of images. That cuts the cost of a personalized environment from thousands of dollars to well under $100 of compute.
revenue_model: Per-scene fees, community subscriptions for scene libraries and refreshes, hospice partnerships, and a consumer gift channel for diaspora families.
non_obvious_insight: Reminiscence works best when it is specific and shared, and personalization used to cost too much. The most valuable scenes are not beautiful cities but the ordinary corner, kitchen and street a person actually lived on.
first_30_days: Offer 10 memory-care communities three free scenes each, generated from residents' family photos. Track engagement and agitation logs with staff, then sell five-scene packs at $500 and add one hospice partner.

title: Night-Shift Bench Techs for Time-Critical Experiments
one_liner: An agency of vetted, laid-off bench technicians who show up at 2 a.m. or on Christmas morning to harvest time points, feed cells and load overnight runs from the lab's own protocol cards, with photo proof and a break-glass line to the postdoc.
customer: Small private biotechs and startups in shared lab space (LabCentral-type incubators and coworking labs), plus soft-money academic labs with reagent or staffing budgets and industry-funded academic labs. Billed at $85-120/hour with a 2-hour minimum. The incubator or landlord earns a referral fee.
problem: Biology runs on its own clock. 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. time-course harvests, weekend and holiday cell feeding, 48-hour induction windows and overnight instrument runs are the hidden cost of every wet-lab career. Postdocs cover them with sleep debt, guilt-based favors from grad students, or driving in on Christmas. The person who could do it is often laid off, but a lab will not hand $40k of iPSC-derived cells to a stranger, and access badges and insurance make casual help impossible.
solution: A W-2 (employer-of-record) pool of experienced techs, aseptic-technique certified and proven on a practice run, working from the customer's 'protocol cards'. Each shift is a fixed product: Time-Point Harvest, Weekend Split and Feed, Holiday Cover, Overnight Run Loader. Each has a checklist, timestamped photos at every step, a pre-shift 30-minute video walkthrough, and a break-glass contact. Sitters first do a 'dry run' on the customer's cheap spare line. Incubator and coworking-lab operators put the agency on an approved-vendor list, which solves badge and insurance access once for hundreds of labs.
why_now: A large pool of experienced bench techs and postdocs has been released by biotech layoffs since 2023 and funding disruption in 2025-26. Lean startups have fewer people per experiment, so time-critical work lands on founders. Bigger time-course, organoid and perturbation experiments driven by AI-bio data demand make odd-hour work more frequent. Shared-lab operators want more amenities to fill vacant benches.
revenue_model: A markup on billed hours (techs are paid about $40-55/hour, the agency bills $85-120). Monthly retainer for guaranteed availability (for example 'holiday cover pass'). Referral revenue share from shared-lab operators.
non_obvious_insight: The hard constraint is trust, not skill. Nobody outsources their cells because failure is invisible until weeks later. So the product is really an evidence-and-liability wrapper: photo proof, protocol cards, dry runs, and operator pre-approval. Also, the early customers are not academia (IACUC, badges and university procurement kill it) but private benches in rented lab space, where one operator agreement unlocks dozens of labs.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 recently laid-off techs through personal networks and biotech alumni groups. Get a business license, a staffing or PEO partner for payroll, and general liability insurance. Call the community managers at 2-3 shared-lab spaces in one city and offer the first holiday-cover week free. Sell the first paid 3 a.m. harvest to a founder who is already doing it themselves. Turn every job into a reusable protocol card. Aim for about 10 recurring customers by month 6.

title: Entry-Integrity Layer for Contests and Festivals
one_liner: Intake screening and a finalist verification desk for photo, film, screenplay and art open calls that fear an AI-winner scandal.
customer: Organizers of photo contests, film festivals, screenwriting and comics competitions, and art open calls, especially those that already collect entry fees through FilmFreeway, Submittable or their own forms.
problem: Generative tools make entries free to produce, so organizers face reviewer overload and reputational risk from an AI-made winner. Platform stigma around AI content has just hardened (TIDAL, Snap, Spotify, YouTube all acted between May and Aug 2026), so a scandal now costs more. Organizers verify nothing beyond a checkbox.
solution: A plugin or service that (1) screens each entry on intake with C2PA and SynthID checks, metadata analysis and a detector ensemble, sorting entries into green, amber and red for screeners, (2) asks finalists for a proof pack (raw files, project files or a behind-the-scenes clip), and (3) runs a 48-hour human-reviewed finalist verification that yields a 'Verified Human-Made Finalist' certificate for the winners' announcement. High-volume calls can add a refundable deposit.
why_now: Provenance signals are now common in cameras and tools, detector prices have fallen, and AI-content policies are stricter across platforms, so organizers finally have something to check against and something to lose.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per-entry surcharge or $500-5,000 per contest, plus $20-60 per verified finalist, renewing annually.
non_obvious_insight: Organizers already charge entry fees, so a $1 integrity fee is invisible to entrants. Only the top 1-3% of entries need deep verification, and the real buyer motive is insurance against one embarrassing scandal.
first_30_days: List 50 mid-size contests with deadlines in Q4-Q1 from FilmFreeway and photo-contest calendars. Offer free finalist verification to the first five in exchange for a case study, run it as a concierge service with tools behind it, then charge $1,500 flat.

title: One Recert: Housing Paperwork Keeps Medicaid Coverage
one_liner: Reuse the income and employment paperwork affordable-housing operators already collect every year to stop residents' Medicaid from lapsing under the new work requirements, paid per retained member by Medicaid health plans.
customer: Medicaid managed-care organizations in expansion states (pay per retained member-month or per completed redetermination), plus LIHTC/HUD affordable-housing owners (pay per unit for lower delinquency and turnover). Hospitals in expansion states are a third payer.
problem: Work requirements hit all 41 expansion states on Jan 1, 2027 (Nebraska has been live since May 1, 2026), with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit to hospitals. Losses are mostly paperwork failures rather than true ineligibility (Arkansas's 2018 experiment saw about 18,000 people drop off largely through reporting failures). Each lost member is lost capitation for the plan, unpaid bills for the hospital and, later, a late-rent risk for the landlord.
solution: With resident consent, ingest the annual and interim income/employment verifications that housing operators already gather. Map them to state rules (80 hours a month, or roughly $580 in monthly income, plus exemptions such as caregivers), build the compliance packet, submit it to the state portal or plan, and send monthly nudges when hours dip. A remote call team plus the property's resident-services coordinator handles the human steps.
why_now: The Jan 1, 2027 nationwide deadline is three months away and plans are setting 2027 retention budgets now. Nebraska is a live proving ground today. ACA subsidy expiry already added about 4.8M uninsured, so plans and hospitals are hunting for any lever that keeps members covered.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month retention fee or $75-150 per completed redetermination from plans; $2-4/unit/month SaaS from housing owners; hospital-funded pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Affordable-housing recertification is the most audit-grade employment and income record low-income adults have, and nobody reuses it. The housing operator is also the only party that sees the resident monthly and has its own reason to care, since Medicaid loss leads to medical debt and then late rent.
first_30_days: Start in Nebraska. Sign one affordable operator with 1,000-3,000 units and one Medicaid plan. Hand-build the packet workflow with forms and spreadsheets for 100 consenting residents, measure retention against a comparison group, and price the service per retained member. Clone state by state ahead of Jan 1.

title: Robot Pilot Guild for Gaming-Native Gen Z
one_liner: A guild that recruits, trains and certifies gamers aged 16-25 to remotely pilot delivery robots and humanoids, with a portable verified flight-hour logbook that becomes their credential.
customer: Robotics and physical-AI companies (sidewalk delivery, warehouse, humanoid pilots) that buy validated pilot-hours and demonstration data. Workforce boards and trainees pay for certification.
problem: Robots in 2026 run on human backup: remote assistance for stuck delivery robots and teleoperated demonstrations to train humanoids. Companies staff this ad hoc through BPOs and labeling vendors, with high churn, uneven quality and no career ladder. US lab teleoperator roles are already posting at $30-$55 per hour. Gen Alpha and Gen Z raised on controllers have the reflexes but no legitimate on-ramp.
solution: Regional 'pilot houses' with standardized rigs plus at-home certification. A tiered license runs from Level 1 sidewalk assist to Level 3 dexterous manipulation, tested in simulation and on real robots. The guild is the W-2 employer of record, sells SLA-bound pilot capacity by the validated hour, and records verified hours in a portable logbook like aviation. Quality is managed through replay review and per-task acceptance rates.
why_now: Teleoperation sits at the center of humanoid and home-robot programs in 2026 (home humanoids such as 1X NEO ship with remote operators), and demonstration data is being bought like compute. Entry-level white-collar hiring is weak, so young people want alternative on-ramps. Robot companies need reliable operator supply now, not in 2030.
revenue_model: $25-$45 per validated pilot-hour billed to robot companies, targeting about 40% gross margin. Certification fees of $200-$600 paid by trainees, workforce funds or employers, plus placement fees when companies hire pilots directly.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset in physical AI is consistent, high-quality human motor demonstration, and Gen Alpha has been practicing exactly that skill for a decade. A verified flight-hour logbook turns play into a portable credential. That makes workers stickier and quality auditable, so this is a licensed guild employer rather than a gig marketplace.
first_30_days: Approach three sidewalk-delivery or warehouse-robot startups with visible remote-assist queues. Offer a paid 4-week pilot with 10 trained gamers recruited from Discord communities and community-college esports programs. Train them on the customer's own simulator and bill per validated hour. Goal: one signed pilot and one letter of intent for a 50-pilot cohort.

title: Farmer-Photo Crop Insurance Verification
one_liner: Replace satellite guesswork with dense, fraud-checked farmer photos, read by locally trained crop models, to trigger insurance payouts.
customer: Agricultural insurers and reinsurers, agri-input companies and cooperatives in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.
problem: Western models fail spectacularly on African crops, index insurance has high basis risk, and manual claim verification costs more than a smallholder premium.
solution: A local crop-damage model trained on image datasets (one project has 5M+ crop images) that takes geo-tagged WhatsApp photos, cross-checks neighbouring farms and weather, and triggers mobile-money payouts. The wedge is one maize or coffee cooperative with one insurer.
why_now: Local crop datasets and small on-device models exist now, and FarmerChat has answered 8M+ farmer questions, so farmers already talk to AI on their phones.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per policy per season for verification, or a share of premium.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is solved by dense ground truth from the insured themselves, not by better satellites.
first_30_days: Partner with a cooperative of about 2,000 farmers and run photo verification in parallel with existing claims for one season.

title: Youth-Slang Drift API for Safety Teams
one_liner: A continuously updated, human-verified lexicon and drift detector for Gen Alpha and teen slang, coded risk terms and grooming language, sold as an API to moderation and school-safety teams.
customer: Trust-and-safety teams at game and social platforms, K-12 student-monitoring vendors, school-safety directors, and moderation stacks inside AI toys and companions.
problem: Youth language shifts every few months. Classifiers trained on last year's data misread banter and miss coded terms for sextortion, self-harm and grooming. School monitors bury counselors in false alerts. As bans push kids into private chats and games, moderation teams are older and further from the language.
solution: A lexicon with context tags (benign, hazard, coded-risk; severity; platform of origin; age range), plus alerts when a term's usage or meaning shifts, delivered via API and a weekly briefing. It is built with a paid panel of consented 16-19-year-old language scouts (parental consent where needed) and linguists.
why_now: Age-gated platform tiers, bans and duty-of-care laws raise the cost of missed threats. Moderation is now LLM-based and needs fresh context that models lack. Volume and speed of Gen Alpha slang keep growing.
revenue_model: $2-15k a month per platform or vendor for API and briefings, plus custom lexicon builds.
non_obvious_insight: LLMs know last year's slang, so freshness is a data-supply problem. The moat is the paid youth panel and labeling process, not the model.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 teens (with parental consent) and 3 linguists. Publish a free monthly 'Gen Alpha threat lexicon' for trust-and-safety newsletters. Land 2 design partners, one school-monitoring vendor and one kids' game, at $1k a month each.

title: Backyard Telescopes as Cubesat Finders
one_liner: Pay owners of consumer smart telescopes to image newly deployed smallsats, so operators learn which object is theirs and whether their panels deployed.
customer: University teams, startups and small operators flying on rideshare missions with 100+ payloads, plus satellite insurers and brokers who want an independent health signal.
problem: After rideshare deployments the public catalog lags days to weeks and objects are mis-associated. A silent satellite may be dead or merely misidentified, and operators without their own ground networks burn weeks of contact attempts. 2025 saw 321 orbital launches and 4,517 satellites deployed, so far more unfunded small operators face this.
solution: A client for popular smart telescopes (Seestar and Unistellar class) receives tasking for predicted twilight passes and uploads wide-field frames. The server solves streak astrometry and photometry, returning position updates to improve the operator's orbit, an ID confirmation, and tumble rate and brightness changes that hint at panel or antenna deployment. Owners are paid credits per validated pass, with leaderboards.
why_now: Rideshare cadence and cheap launch flood the catalog with small, poorly funded payloads. Thousands of app-controlled smart telescopes now sit in backyards, AI streak detection is cheap, and the brief flags rising conjunction-screening load for operators.
revenue_model: $1,500-4,000 per mission for a LEOP identification and deployment package, plus a $500 per month monitoring subscription. About a third of revenue goes to observer payouts, and insurers pay per-object fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a fast, independent 'is it alive and deployed?' second opinion, not images. Space-situational-awareness firms build expensive sensor networks, whereas hobbyists supply sensors that are paid for in status and gear credits, at a fraction of the cost.
first_30_days: Use open-source astrometry and streak tools. Recruit 150 smart-telescope owners in maker forums and Discords. Take the public payload list of the next rideshare mission, cold-email 3 small operators with a free pilot, and convert two to paid at $1,500 on the following mission.

title: Skin-Tone-Verified SpO2 Validation Cooperative
one_liner: Build the 10x-larger, objectively skin-tone-measured, arterial-blood-paired dataset that pulse-oximeter and wearable makers need, and sell access, bias reports and validation studies.
customer: Pulse-oximeter and wearable OEMs and startups, plus hospital purchasing groups that want independent bias reports before buying devices.
problem: Current pulse oximeters tend to overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients, so low oxygen can go undetected. A new arXiv correction method works on 98 patients from the public OpenOximetry Repository but the authors say a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed for significance. The 2013 FDA 510(k) guidance asks for only 'at least 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of your subject pool' and says nothing of objective pigmentation measures.
solution: Recruit a diverse cohort and characterize each participant with a skin reflectance spectrometer to get melanin fraction. Run induced-hypoxia studies with paired arterial samples through partner university hypoxia labs. License the de-identified dataset and calibration models to OEMs, and offer per-device bias validation and a public 'bias report card' for hospital buyers.
why_now: The 2026 arXiv paper by Blaney, Fantini, Koomson and colleagues shows a melanin-aware correction that cut error from +2.8 to +0.1 percentage points per unit melanin fraction, but it is data-limited. Wearable SpO2 features are now mainstream, and regulators and buyers are asking for skin-tone-diverse evidence. I could not verify in this session the status of the January 2025 FDA draft guidance, so confirm it before pitching.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses of roughly $50-250k, per-device validation studies of $100-400k, and annual bias-report subscriptions for hospital groups and OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is data, not algorithms. The arXiv paper says current oximeters 'overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients', its correction relies on per-patient skin-tone measurement, and 'a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30122). The current FDA 510(k) guidance sets a low bar of 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of the pool (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/pulse-oximeters-premarket-notification-submissions-510ks-guidance-industry-and-food-and-drug). Whoever owns the largest objectively measured dataset sets the de facto standard, and every OEM has to buy or replicate it.
first_30_days: Email the arXiv authors and OpenOximetry contributors about their data needs. Sign a partner hypoxia lab and an IRB pathway, and design a 30-50 participant pilot. Pre-sell the pilot dataset to 3 wearable or oximeter startups through LOIs. Prototype a spectrometer-based melanin measurement protocol and publish a pre-registered study plan.

title: Marginalia: Lived-Experience Annotated Books
one_liner: One-of-one physical books annotated in ink by people who have actually lived what the book is about, such as a retired ER nurse in The Plague or a lighthouse keeper's daughter in To the Lighthouse.
customer: Gift buyers and collectors paying $250-1,200 per copy, quarterly-subscription readers ($180/quarter), independent bookstores, libraries and special collections, and professional associations gifting to retirees.
problem: Explanations and summaries are free and infinite, so 'I've read it' signals nothing. Celebrity-signed copies signal fame, not thought. What is scarce is a particular lived mind reading a text in real time: dated, physical, opinionated, and accountable.
solution: Recruit about 100 'readers of record': retired judges, surgeons, sommeliers, deep-sea divers, and translators. Match each to a canonical book that fits their life. Each annotates a physical copy under a fixed protocol: at least 60 marginal notes, a two-page flyleaf letter, a signed colophon, and a one-take authenticity video. Copies are numbered and sold. A commission tier lets you order a book annotated by someone in your recipient's own profession (a retirement gift for a fire chief). Displaced translators can annotate a translation against the original, showing what the machine misses.
why_now: AI summarizers have made shallow reading free, so deep, lived reading is the differentiator. The 2026 human-made premium is well documented. Physical-book culture is holding up, and the 'association copy' idea is old and understood among collectors.
revenue_model: Per-copy sales (reader 40%, platform about 45%, materials about 15%), a quarterly subscription, institutional acquisitions, and annual charity auctions of 'famous minds' copies.
non_obvious_insight: In an age of infinite explanation, the scarce good is witnessed subjectivity. A marginal note is a physical, un-averaged opinion, the opposite of what a language model produces. Collectors already pay premiums for association copies (a book owned or annotated by someone notable). This manufactures them prospectively and at scale.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 readers through retirement communities and professional associations. Produce 30 copies. Sell through a Substack with page photos and pre-orders. Approach 5 indie bookstores for consignment. Goal: $10k in pre-orders by day 60.

title: Funeral Committee Escrow and Fixed-Price Vendor Network
one_liner: A per-funeral M-Pesa vault where contributions can only be released to pre-priced vendors with two-of-three committee approvals, ending the 'where did the burial money go' fights.
customer: The family and burial committee (treasurer, chair, village elder, workplace welfare group) organising a rural funeral, usually with a Nairobi or diaspora fundraising arm. Vendors (tent and chair hire, caterers, coffin makers, embalmers, hearse and PA operators) are the second paying side.
problem: A rural funeral is often a family's biggest single cash event, drawing hundreds of mourners and costing multiples of a year's farm income. It is run on WhatsApp groups and an exercise book. Treasurer fraud and 'the money vanished' accusations are common and can split families for years. Vendors quote inflated prices to grieving families who cannot shop around, mortuary storage fees accrue daily so decisions are rushed, and families often sell land, borrow against coop shares or take mobile loans to close the gap. Existing crowdfunding tools collect money but do nothing about how it is spent.
solution: Each funeral gets a dynamic M-Pesa paybill account and a WhatsApp bot (English, Swahili, Sheng). The committee picks from fixed-price packages (basic, standard, large) with vendor prices published. Every payout to a vendor till needs two of three designated approvers by USSD PIN, and a live ledger is visible to all contributors. The bot also handles pledge tracking, reminders in the Nairobi and home committees, the mortuary and transport schedule, and a post-funeral accounting statement. Money sits in a licensed payment provider's trust account, not on the startup's balance sheet.
why_now: M-Pesa paybill, till and B2B payout APIs are mature enough to make programmable escrow cheap, and the WhatsApp Business API is inexpensive. LLMs now let a bot handle Swahili and Sheng committee chatter. The post-2023 cost-of-living squeeze makes families more sensitive to funeral overspending and to selling land to pay for it. Funeral crowdfunding has trained diaspora and urban Kenyans to give online, but nobody controls the spend side.
revenue_model: About 2-3% fee on money flowing through the vault plus negotiated vendor margins or referral commissions of roughly 8-12% on vendor spend. Later upsells are funeral cover (partnered with a licensed insurer), memorial pages, and body-transport routing between Nairobi and up-country.
non_obvious_insight: Money that is locked to named vendors is welcome, not resented: it protects the treasurer from the 'sharing tax' of relatives and neighbours asking for cash, and from accusations. In effect the product sells social protection, not payments. Funerals are also where families mortgage their long-term farm assets, so reducing funeral overspend is a farm-resilience product that VCs would never classify as agtech.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 vendors (tents, catering, coffins, hearse) along one corridor such as Nairobi to Murang'a or Nyeri and agree fixed package prices. Onboard the first 5 funerals by offering free setup through church welfare groups, alumni groups and your own contacts, using a manual approval flow on top of an existing paybill provider. Charge the fee only after a funeral closes with a clean statement, and use those statements as proof for the next 50.

title: Beneficiary-Funded Dynamic Line Ratings
one_liner: Skip the utility's missing incentive: let the data center or generator that needs capacity pay for dynamic line ratings and take a slice of the capacity released.
customer: Data center developers and congestion-constrained renewable, storage and merchant generation owners. The utility is a passive partner.
problem: Dynamic line rating adds 30-50% capacity at about a tenth of the cost of reconductoring, but utilities earn no return on operating savings, so adoption is stuck. Projects held back by a few constrained lines lose years or revenue.
solution: A special-purpose company funds and deploys DLR (sensors plus weather-model virtual ratings) on the specific lines limiting a beneficiary's project. A three-party agreement has the utility accept ratings with a safety margin and keep the reliability data, the beneficiary gets earlier energization or less curtailment, and the company earns a capacity-uplift fee for about 10 years.
why_now: Automated study tools (Tapestry ran ~220 GW of PJM applications in under an hour) show speed is possible. FERC's ambient-adjusted ratings rule and GETs consideration laws mainstream the concept. Cost of delay is enormous.
revenue_model: Cost-plus up-front sensors and analytics, plus an annual $/kW capacity-uplift fee or a share of avoided curtailment.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for the utility's incentive to change, and it will not. Contract the incentive from the customer instead. That is structurally a customer-funded upgrade, which utilities already know how to accept.
first_30_days: Use public congestion and rating data to find the 20 lines most limiting renewables and large loads. Sell three $25-60k congestion and rating audits to constrained project owners. Recruit one utility engineering champion. Resell sensors from an existing DLR vendor.
